title: Irena Sendler: a quiet hero
text:
For decades, very few people knew the name Irena Sendler. Today she is remembered as one of the bravest women of the Second World War, a social worker who helped to save around 2,500 Jewish children from the Warsaw Ghetto.

Irena was born in 1910 in Warsaw and grew up in Otwock, a town where her father worked as a doctor. He treated poor patients, many of them Jewish, often without asking for payment. When he died of typhus caught from a patient, Irena was only seven. She later said that his most important lesson was simple: if you see someone drowning, you must jump into the water to help, even if you cannot swim.

When the Germans created the ghetto in 1940, Irena was working for the city's social welfare department. Because her job gave her a permit to enter the ghetto to check for infectious diseases, she was able to go in and out. Together with a group of colleagues from the underground organisation Żegota, she began to smuggle children out – in ambulances, through sewers, hidden in boxes and suitcases, or through a church that had entrances on both sides of the ghetto wall.

The children were given new, Polish names and placed with families, in convents and in orphanages. Irena wrote down their real names on thin pieces of paper and buried them in glass jars in a friend's garden, hoping that one day the children could be reunited with their families.

In October 1943, she was arrested by the Gestapo. She was tortured but refused to give any names. She was sentenced to death, but Żegota managed to bribe a guard, and she escaped on the way to her execution. She spent the rest of the war in hiding, still helping others.

After the war, the communist authorities did not celebrate her work, and her story was almost forgotten. It became famous only in 1999, when a group of American schoolgirls wrote a play about her. Irena died in 2008, at the age of 98. She always insisted that she was not a hero. "I could have done more," she said.
